reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: The commonest autoimmune blistering disease, typically affecting older adults
Classically produces large, tense, fluid-filled blisters on an erythematous or urticarial base, favouring the trunk, flexures, and limbs
Blisters are tense and relatively robust because the split is subepidermal, unlike the fragile flaccid blisters of pemphigus
A prodromal phase of intense itch with urticarial or eczematous plaques may precede blistering by weeks or months and is easily misdiagnosed
Mucosal involvement is uncommon and usually mild, which helps distinguish it from pemphigus vulgaris
Diagnosis is confirmed by subepidermal blistering on histology and linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence
Management uses potent topical corticosteroids for localised disease and systemic corticosteroids or steroid-sparing immunomodulators for widespread involvement
Consider a drug trigger, since certain medications (including some diabetes and immunotherapy agents) can precipitate pemphigoid
reference.pathophysiology: Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies directed against hemidesmosomal proteins of the dermal-epidermal junction, principally BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells, particularly eosinophils, which release proteases that degrade the anchoring structures holding the epidermis to the dermis. This produces a subepidermal split, giving tense blisters with an intact epidermal roof. The urticarial prodrome reflects the inflammatory phase before frank blistering. Disease predominates in the elderly and may be associated with neurological disease and, in some cases, drug exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Pemphigus vulgaris (flaccid blisters, mucosal erosions, intraepidermal split)
Urticaria or eczema during the non-bullous prodromal phase
additionalInvestigations: Lesional skin biopsy showing a subepidermal blister with eosinophils
Perilesional direct immunofluorescence showing linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone
Serum indirect immunofluorescence and ELISA for BP180 and BP230 antibodies
Salt-split skin studies to localise antibody binding when distinguishing from related disorders
Review of medication history for possible drug-induced pemphigoid
redFlags: Extensive blistering with widespread skin barrier loss and secondary infection risk
Signs of sepsis or systemic deterioration, particularly in frail elderly patients
Complications of systemic corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy
Rapidly progressive disease unresponsive to initial treatment
reference.prognosis: Bullous pemphigoid is often a self-limiting disease over months to a few years and generally responds to treatment, but morbidity and mortality are notable in elderly patients, largely driven by comorbidity and treatment-related complications.
pitfalls: Missing the non-bullous urticarial or eczematous prodrome and delaying diagnosis
Confusing it with pemphigus vulgaris and misjudging prognosis and mucosal risk
Over-reliance on high-dose systemic steroids in frail patients when potent topical steroids may suffice
Failing to identify a drug trigger that could be withdrawn
management: Use potent topical corticosteroids such as clobetasol as first-line therapy, which controls even extensive disease with fewer systemic effects in frail elderly patients
Add systemic corticosteroids for widespread or resistant disease, tapering to the lowest effective dose once controlled

Employ steroid-sparing adjuncts including doxycycline with or without nicotinamide, and immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate, reserving rituximab or omalizumab for refractory disease
Provide wound care of blisters and erosions with attention to skin hygiene and prevention of secondary infection
Review medication history and withdraw any drug implicated in drug-induced pemphigoid
Monitor for treatment-related complications in the elderly, including infection, hyperglycaemia and osteoporosis, with bone protection during prolonged steroid use
Refer to dermatology and coordinate management of comorbidities, including associated neurological disease
